title: Enolate resonance
subtitle: The enolate of acetone: carbanion and oxyanion forms

carbanion.caption: sodium enolate of acetone, drawn as a carbanion
carbanion.learnerPrompt: Draw the resonance form with the negative charge on oxygen. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
hintTiers: The negative carbon sits next to a C=O group. Where can its lone pair go?
The carbon lone pair makes a C=C π bond. The central carbon cannot have five bonds, so the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the lone pair of the negative carbon into its bond to the carbonyl carbon. Arrow 2: the C=O π bond onto oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Resonance arrows never break or make σ bonds: the atoms stay exactly where they are. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
The oxygen lone pair pushing in would give the carbonyl carbon five bonds, and oxygen has nothing to push towards. The electrons flow from the negative carbon towards oxygen.
The π pair moves towards oxygen, the more electronegative atom, not onto carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: The C=C π bond is right, but the carbonyl carbon now has five bonds. Push the C=O π bond onto oxygen at the same time.

oxyanion.caption: sodium enolate of acetone, drawn as an oxyanion

steps.explanationAfterStep: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so this form, with the charge on oxygen, is the major contributor. No atom has moved: this is not the enol, which has a hydrogen on oxygen. With most carbon electrophiles the enolate still reacts at carbon.

mechanismSummary: The carbanion lone pair forms a C=C π bond, and the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. The form with the charge on oxygen is the major contributor, but both describe one ion, which reacts at carbon or at oxygen.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 7 (Delocalization and conjugation)
